children: is reportedly preparing a massive expansion of its same-day delivery network, targeting more than 1,000 dedicated facilities by 2031 from roughly 85 today. The initiative could push Amazon's fulfillment infrastructure dramatically closer to Prime customers, strengthening its speed advantage against Walmart
, but it also raises the stakes around capital spending and whether faster delivery can generate adequate returns.

The initiative, known internally as Project Mercury, would place dedicated same-day facilities within a 10-mile straight-line radius of 80% of U.S. Prime subscribers by 2031, according to Business Insider.
Amazon currently positions many same-day sites roughly a 90-minute drive from customers.

The expansion would therefore represent a fundamental redesign of the company's fulfillment footprint, allowing more inventory to sit closer to households and potentially lowering the time and distance required for last-mile deliveries.
Amazon's three-year operating plan allocates $6.8 billion toward U.S. same-day capacity during 2026 and 2027.

Internal analysis reportedly estimates Project Mercury could generate $7.1 billion in economic value over a decade and become cash-flow positive by 2030. Some spending could replace investment that otherwise would have gone toward traditional delivery facilities.
An Amazon spokesperson said internal forecasts are "preliminary, subject to significant revision, and shouldn't be treated as finalized plans."
Amazon already says same-day service reaches more than 10,000 cities and towns, although dedicated same-day facilities do not handle every order.
"That said, it's no secret that we're focused on delivering faster for customers and the expansion of our same-day delivery network is playing a big role in that," the spokesperson said.
Project Mercury could widen Amazon's logistics moat, but execution and economics matter more than the headline facility count.
Investors should watch fulfillment costs per unit, delivery speeds, Prime engagement and whether denser same-day infrastructure improves retail margins.

The biggest risk is overbuilding capacity before order density justifies the investment. If Amazon can reach positive cash flow around 2030 while accelerating delivery, the network could strengthen both customer loyalty and competitive positioning. Higher-than-planned construction or operating costs would make the $6.8 billion near-term commitment harder to justify.

title: Amazon's Delivery War Is About to Get Bigger
